Zoe Min Park

life-049 · holdout · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I like a room where people can hear themselves think, but I don't want a small life. Sometimes I'm quiet because I'm tired of listening, and sometimes I'm just deciding what color the cake should be.

  • family: Lives with parents and a younger brother; family members learned basic signing after her hearing loss was identified.
  • finances: Comfortable middle income; hearing technology expenses are planned and sometimes delay holidays.
  • geography: Pearland, Texas, with relatives elsewhere in the Houston area.
  • cultureLanguages: Korean American household using English, Korean with grandparents, and some ASL; she chooses among spoken and signed communication by situation.
  • school: Public high school; bilateral moderate hearing loss accommodated with hearing aids, captions, a remote microphone, and seating choices.
  • accessOpportunities: Has accessible art classes and a regional deaf and hard-of-hearing youth group; some extracurricular spaces remain acoustically difficult.
  • Age 4–5

    Zoe loved helping decorate birthday cakes with uneven stars and carefully chosen colors. Hearing aids were already part of her routine, but she most often described herself as the person who got to choose the sprinkles.

  • Age 6–7

    Her first classroom microphone made lessons easier to follow, while noisy lunch tables remained tiring. One friend began meeting her outside after eating, and they invented sidewalk-chalk games that did not require rapid group conversation.

  • Age 8–9

    She joined a youth group where several communication styles were normal. Seeing older teenagers ask confidently for captions gave her language for requests she had previously left her parents to make on her behalf.

  • Age 10–11

    During remote school she appreciated captions but disliked being expected to watch faces and worksheets simultaneously. Baking with her brother became a welcome activity where written recipes, gestures, and familiar routines worked together.

  • Age 12–13

    She entered a school art show with a series of tiny cake drawings. Praise interested her, yet she also enjoyed calculating how much frosting a real version would need and testing whether colors survived refrigeration.

  • Age 14–15

    Zoe tried student council and discovered that meetings could be accessible when agendas arrived beforehand. She helped organize a quiet study night but declined one loud dance committee, explaining her reasons without withdrawing from everything else.

  • Age 16

    She now bakes for family events, paints, and attends selected council meetings. She is considering Texas postsecondary options with attention to classroom access, but also wants ordinary details—friendly common spaces, useful kitchens, and people who remember to face her.

Life now

  • enjoys: Cake decoration · Painting small objects · Planning welcoming events
  • avoids: Uncaptioned videos · Several overlapping conversations
  • activities: Family baking · Art class · Student council · Youth group
  • demonstratedSkills: Scales recipes · Coordinates event supplies · Requests communication access
  • unfamiliarActivities: Outdoor endurance sports · Electronics repair · Formal acting
  • motivations: Making shared celebrations enjoyable · Choosing participation on her terms
  • ambitions: Interested in continuing education · Imagines a home where friends gather around food and communication access is routine.
  • struggles: Listening fatigue · Others assuming silence means disinterest
  • supports: Family · Access coordinator · Youth peers · Art teacher
  • practicalConstraints: Reliable hearing-device support · Accessible meeting formats · Travel to youth group

Still uncertain: Is event organization enjoyable beyond familiar groups? · Which campus environments reduce fatigue without limiting opportunities?
